overview.intro: The Harappan (Indus Valley) Civilisation, flourishing around 2600-1900 BCE, was one of the world's earliest urban civilisations, spread over the Indus plains and beyond. This chapter studies the archaeological sources through which we know it - the Great Bath, Citadel, seals, the bearded man, the dancing girl, the dockyard, granaries and its undeciphered script - and then examines its remarkable urban planning, trade, art and craft, and the possible reasons for its decline.

blocks.text: The civilisation is called Harappan because Harappa, the first of its sites, was excavated in the 1920s on the river Ravi (now in Pakistan). It covered a vast area - from Manda in Jammu to Daimabad in Maharashtra, and from Sutkagendor on the Makran coast to Alamgirpur on the Hindon - far larger than contemporary Mesopotamia or Egypt. Radiocarbon dating places its mature phase around 2600-1900 BCE. It was a contemporary of the Mesopotamian civilisation, with which it traded by land and sea.

Sources - the Great Bath and the Citadel. The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro is a rectangular tank of baked brick, about 12 m long, with steps leading down on two sides, surrounded by corridors and rooms, and made watertight with bitumen. Its size and isolation suggest communal ritual bathing. The Citadel to its west was a raised citadel bearing the major public structures - the Great Bath, a large granary, and the Kollian-style assembly hall - showing planned separation of public and private space.

Sources - seals, bearded man, dancing girl. Thousands of square steatite seals show animals (bull, unicorn, elephant, rhinoceros, tiger), a seated figure in yogic posture (the 'proto-Shiva'), and short inscriptions; they were used to stamp goods and bales. The 'bearded man' is a small steatite bust from Mohenjo-daro of a dignified bearded figure with a trefoil-decorated shawl - perhaps a priest or king. The bronze 'dancing girl', found at Mohenjo-daro, stands in a tribhanga pose with bangles up her left arm, proving skill in bronze casting by the lost-wax process and giving rare evidence of dance and adornment.

Sources - dockyard, granaries, script. The dockyard at Lothal (Gujarat) is a rectangular basin connected to the old channel of the Sabarmati; its spill-way lock kept ships afloat at low tide, proving maritime trade. Huge granaries - at Harappa a series of brick working-floors and at Mohenjo-daro a raised brick granary with air-ducts - show collection and distribution of surplus grain. The script, seen on seals, pottery and copper tablets, runs right to left (boustrophedon on some), has about 400 signs, and has not been deciphered; without it we rely wholly on archaeology.

Town planning. Harappan cities were built to a grid plan: streets in perfect right angles, running north-south and east-west, cutting the city into rectangular blocks. Houses of baked brick (with standard 1:2:4 brick ratio) had wells, bathrooms with drains connected to covered street drains with soak-pits, and often a courtyard. There were public wells, lamp-posts(?), and a clear division between the raised Citadel and the Lower Town. Drainage - covered drains with sump-pits along every street - was the finest in the ancient world.

Trade. Agricultural surplus fed craft production and trade. Internally, raw materials moved between regions: copper from Rajasthan (Khetri), gold from Karnataka, lapis lazuli from Afghanistan, shell from the coast, and timber from the Himalayan foothills. Externally, seals, weights and Mesopotamian records show trade with Sumer (Mesopotamia, called 'Meluha' in Mesopotamian texts): cotton textiles, beads, shell-work, ivory and timber went out; copper, tin, precious stones came in. Goods moved by ox-carts and river craft and by sea through Lothal's dockyard. Standard weights in the binary (1, 2, 4...) and decimal system, and cubical chert weights, point to organised commerce.

Art and craft. Craftsmen worked in stone, metal, shell, clay and cloth. Sculpture: the bearded man (steatite bust), the bronze dancing girl, and the bull from Mohenjo-daro in metal. The red pottery with black designs (with its fine 'q' ware) was wheel-thrown; painted designs show leaves, birds, fish and geometric patterns. Jewellery of gold, silver, copper, shell and semi-precious beads; children's toys with wheels on carts; the bronze 'bullock cart' model; the famous faience 'priest-king'. Cotton was spun and woven - the earliest known use of cotton in the world. Inlay work, bead-making at Chanhudaro, shell bangles, and metal casting by the lost-wax (cire perdue) method complete the picture.

Decline. By about 1900-1800 BCE the mature civilisation faded. No single cause is accepted; scholars point to: (i) geological and climatic change - tectonic upheavals possibly diverting the Ghaggar-Hakra (often linked with the Saraswati) and drying rivers; (ii) recurrent floods (evidence of silt at Mohenjo-daro); (iii) desiccation and declining rainfall; (iv) overuse of land, deforestation for brick fuel and grazing; (v) possible attacks by outsiders (the old 'Aryan invasion' theory is now doubted, but there is evidence of some violence at certain sites); (vi) breakdown of the trade network with Mesopotamia and internal collapse of the cities' economic base. The cities were abandoned or their culture 'ruralised' - but craft and agricultural traditions carried into later cultures of the region.

items: Daya Ram Sahni - Excavated Harappa (1921) on the Ravi, launching systematic study.
Rakhaldas Banerji (R.D. Banerji) - Excavated Mohenjo-daro (1922) on the Indus.
John Marshall - Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India who announced the discovery of the Indus Civilisation (1924).
S.R. Rao - Excavated Lothal and worked on the script.
Geological and climatic change - possible tectonic uplift diverting rivers such as the Ghaggar-Hakra.
Repeated floods, as shown by silt layers at Mohenjo-daro.
Desiccation - declining rainfall and increasing aridity.
Deforestation and overgrazing to feed brick kilns and cattle.
Disruption of long-distance trade with Mesopotamia.
Possible external attacks at some sites (a debated factor).
Abandonment of the great cities; population moved east and south.
Loss of writing, weights, standard brick size and urban amenities.
Ruralisation: cities gave way to villages and pastoral camps.
Survival of some techniques (cotton weaving, pottery, bead-making) in successor cultures.

blocks.text: Citadel vs Lower Town: Raised western public zone with the Great Bath and granary versus lower eastern residential blocks on the grid plan.
Seal vs Script: Seals are carved stamp artefacts used on goods, versus the writing system which appears on seals but remains undeciphered.
Harappan vs Mesopotamian: Contemporary civilisations, but Harappa used standard baked brick, grid planning and covered drains, and traded with Sumer.

items: Calling it only the 'Indus Valley' civilisation - sites like Dholavira and Daimabad lie far beyond the Indus basin.
Saying the script has been deciphered - it has not; readings remain unproven.
Confusing the Great Bath (Mohenjo-daro) with the dockyard (Lothal).
Claiming a single cause (e.g. only floods) for the decline - the syllabus and evidence point to several overlapping causes.
Attributing the 'dancing girl' to Harappa instead of Mohenjo-daro.

keyPoints: Sources: Bath, Citadel, seals, bearded man, dancing girl, dockyard, granaries, script.
Planning: grid streets, baked bricks (1:2:4), covered drains, Citadel + Lower Town.
Art: dancing girl, bearded man, painted pottery, beads, cotton.
Decline: climate/floods/river shift + deforestation + trade collapse.
examFocus: Also called the Indus Valley Civilisation; mature phase c. 2600-1900 BCE.
Discovered through excavations in 1921-22 (Sahni, Banerji; announced by Marshall).
Great Bath (Mohenjo-daro): ritual bathing; bitumen-lined tank with steps.
Lothal dockyard: tidal basin with spill-way, linking to overseas trade.
Seals: steatite, square, with animals and undeciphered script (~400 signs).
The bronze dancing girl and steatite bearded man are Mohenjo-daro finds.
Standard brick ratio 1:2:4; grid streets; covered drains with soak-pits.
Weight system: binary and decimal; cubical chert weights.
Earliest cotton cultivation/weaving known in the world.
Trade with Mesopotamia ('Meluha'); lapis lazuli from Badakhshan.
Decline: multi-causal - climate, floods, river shifts, deforestation, trade collapse.

vocabulary.meaning: The raised, walled western part of a Harappan city holding important public buildings like the Great Bath or granary.
The larger eastern part of the city with brick houses of ordinary residents.
A large public water tank at Mohenjo-daro, probably used for ritual bathing.
An enclosed basin at Lothal for berthing and servicing ships, showing overseas trade.
A large storehouse for grain, showing surplus production and state control of food.
A small carved stone tablet (usually steatite) pressed on goods to mark ownership; thousands have been found.
The Harappan writing of about 400 signs, found on seals; it remains undeciphered.
Not applicable here; do not confuse with later Iron Age burials (Sangam chapter).

questions.prompt: The Great Bath is a famous structure of which Harappan site?
questions.explanation: The Great Bath - a brick-lined ritual tank - was found at Mohenjo-daro.
questions.commonMistake: Placing it at Harappa or Lothal.

questions.prompt: The dockyard of the Harappan Civilisation was discovered at:
questions.explanation: Lothal's tidal basin with a spill-way is the celebrated dockyard.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing the dockyard with the Great Bath.

questions.prompt: Which material was most commonly used for Harappan seals?
questions.explanation: Seals were mostly square steatite tablets, often fired to a white finish.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing bronze, used for figures not seals.

questions.prompt: Name the two parts into which a Harappan city was divided.
questions.answer: The Citadel (raised western public zone) and the Lower Town (residential).
questions.explanation: A planned division typical of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa.
questions.commonMistake: Naming the tinais or later terms.

questions.prompt: What is the standard brick ratio of Harappan construction?
questions.explanation: Uniform bricks across the civilisation show standardisation.

questions.prompt: What does the dockyard at Lothal reveal about the Harappans?
questions.answer: It shows they practiced maritime trade: the enclosed tidal basin, with its spill-way lock, let ships berth at all tides, so goods could be shipped overseas - linking the civilisation to Mesopotamia and coastal ports.
questions.commonMistake: Describing it as a water tank for bathing.

questions.prompt: Mention any two features of the urban planning of Harappan cities.
questions.answer: Any two of: grid-plan streets at right angles; baked bricks of standard 1:2:4 ratio; covered drains with soak-pits along streets; wells and bathrooms in houses; clear division between Citadel and Lower Town.
questions.explanation: Pick any two concrete features with detail.

questions.prompt: What is the importance of the 'dancing girl' as a source?
questions.answer: The bronze dancing girl of Mohenjo-daro, cast by the lost-wax process, proves skill in metal casting; her bangles and pose give rare evidence of dance, adornment and the status of women in Harappan culture.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing her with the bearded man or naming her a priestess.

questions.prompt: Why is the Harappan Civilisation also called an urban civilisation? Give reasons.
questions.answer: Because it shows all the marks of true urban life: planned cities on a grid; citadels with public buildings; standardised baked-brick houses with private wells and bathrooms; covered street drains with soak-pits; granaries storing surplus; craft quarters and bead factories; standard weights and seals for commerce; and a dockyard for overseas trade. Such complexity of housing, sanitation, storage and trade is possible only in developed urban economies.
questions.explanation: Reasons must cover planning, sanitation, storage, trade.
questions.commonMistake: Listing artefacts without linking to urbanism.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the Citadel and the Lower Town of a Harappan city.
questions.answer: The Citadel was the raised, fortified western part containing major public buildings - the Great Bath, the granary, assembly halls - suggesting civic/ritual authority. The Lower Town was the larger eastern residential area, laid out on the grid plan, with ordinary baked-brick houses, wells, bathrooms and lanes connected to covered drains. The Citadel was elevated and public; the Lower Town, lower and domestic - yet both were walled and planned.
questions.commonMistake: Saying only rulers lived in the Citadel without evidence.

questions.prompt: Discuss the possible causes of the decline of the Harappan Civilisation.
questions.answer: No single cause explains the decline (c. 1900-1800 BCE); most scholars see a combination: (1) Climatic change and desiccation - declining rainfall making the region arid; (2) Geological disturbances - tectonic uplift possibly diverting rivers such as the Ghaggar-Hakra, starving cities of water; (3) Recurrent floods - silt layers at Mohenjo-daro show repeated inundation; (4) Ecological overuse - deforestation for brick kilns and grazing, exhausting soils; (5) Collapse of trade - the breakdown of commerce with Mesopotamia undermined the urban economy; (6) Possible external attacks at some sites, though the old 'Aryan invasion' theory is now doubted. The result was not sudden destruction but a gradual ruralisation: cities emptied, writing and weights disappeared, and populations drifted east and south. This multi-causal view fits the archaeological evidence best.
questions.explanation: Give several causes plus the ruralisation outcome.

questions.prompt: A new Harappan site shows a massive walled tank, rows of small square stone tablets with animal carvings, and a long basin connected to a river channel. What functions would you infer, and why?
questions.answer: The tank suggests ritual or public bathing like the Great Bath; the square carved tablets are seals, indicating ownership marks and trade; the river-connected basin indicates a dockyard or water-management structure, implying riverine or maritime commerce. Together they suggest a trading settlement with organised civic-religious life, as at Lothal and Mohenjo-daro.
questions.explanation: Apply known source-types to new evidence.
questions.commonMistake: Not connecting the basin to trade.
